title: Ruy Lopez for White
description: Learn the Ruy Lopez with the white pieces: the idea of the bishop on b5, the Morphy Defence, the Closed plan, the Exchange Variation, a short look at the Berlin and Open lines, and one trap to avoid.

chapters.title: Berlin, Open Spanish and a trap

lessons.title: The idea of the Ruy Lopez

moves.comment: Now the knight on c6 is under pressure. For now it is safe, but White plays for the long game.

steps.intro: The idea in one sentence: the bishop pressures the knight on c6, which guards the e5 pawn.

moves.comment: The Ruy Lopez.

hints: Use your bishop on f1.
Move it to b5, so it points at the knight on c6.
steps.intro: White to move. Start the Ruy Lopez: put the bishop on the square that pressures the c6 knight.
The bishop on b5 looks along a diagonal at the knight on c6. That knight guards the e5 pawn.

points: The Ruy Lopez is also called the Spanish Game
The bishop does not win a pawn at once. It adds slow pressure
The knight on c6 guards the e5 pawn, so pressure on c6 is pressure on e5
Ask: what could White do on e5 if the c6 knight went away?
mistakes: Thinking Bb5 threatens to win the knight right now. It does not, because the knight is defended
Trading on c6 without a plan
Forgetting to castle after the bishop move
questions: Which black piece does the bishop on b5 point at?
Which black pawn does that knight protect?
Why is slow pressure still useful?

moves.comment: The Morphy Defence.
The bishop retreats but still points at c6.
Black attacks the e4 pawn.
White castles and gets the king safe.

steps.intro: Black asks the bishop a question with 3...a6. White's answer is to keep the bishop on the same diagonal.

moves.comment: The bishop is safe and keeps the pressure.

hints: Use your bishop.
Move it one square along the same diagonal, to a4.
steps.intro: White to move. The pawn on a6 attacks your bishop. Retreat it one square along the same diagonal, so it still points at the c6 knight.

moves.comment: The king is safe and the rook comes to the middle.

hints: Use your king.
Castle on the short side, so the king goes to g1.
steps.intro: White to move. Get your king safe by castling.

hints: Open with the king's pawn, then the knight, then the bishop to b5.
When the a-pawn asks, retreat the bishop to a4.
Finish by castling.
steps.intro: Play the Morphy Defence line as White.

points: 3...a6 is the most common reply. It is called the Morphy Defence
Black asks the bishop what it wants to do
Retreating to a4 keeps the pressure on c6
After 5.O-O White is ready; the e4 pawn is not a worry yet
mistakes: 4.Bxc6 is the Exchange Variation, a different plan; 4.Ba4 keeps the tension.
Moving the bishop to c4 and losing the pressure on c6
Leaving the king in the middle
questions: What is the little pawn on a6 asking the bishop?
Why is a4 a good retreat?
Why do we castle on move five?

moves.comment: Black develops the bishop and prepares to castle.
The rook backs up the e4 pawn.
Black attacks the bishop.
The bishop steps back to a safe square.
This prepares the central push d4.
A small pawn move that takes g4 away from Black's bishop.

steps.intro: The Closed Spanish. White builds step by step. Watch the job of each move.

hints: After castling, put a rook on e1.
When the b-pawn attacks the bishop, go to b3.
Then play the pawn moves c3 and h3.
steps.intro: Play the Closed Spanish main plan as White.

points: This is the classic main line. Both sides build slowly
Black plays ...Be7 and ...O-O; White plays Re1, Bb3, c3 and h3
Each move has a job: Re1 backs up e4, Bb3 saves the bishop, c3 prepares d4, h3 stops a pin
Names from the openings list: Ruy Lopez: Closed
mistakes: Skipping Re1 and leaving e4 weak
Forgetting to retreat the bishop to b3 after ...b5
Playing d4 before c3 is ready
questions: Why does White play Re1?
Where does the bishop go when b5 attacks it?
What does the c3 pawn prepare?

steps.intro: Four moves, four jobs. The rook on e1 guards e4. The bishop on b3 is safe. The c3 pawn prepares d4. The next move, h3, will stop ...Bg4.

moves.comment: The rook looks at e4 and stays in the middle.

hints: Use a rook.
Move the f1 rook to e1.
steps.intro: White to move. Back up the e4 pawn with a rook move.

moves.comment: Now ...Bg4 would just lose the bishop to hxg4.

hints: Use a pawn on the kingside.
Move the h-pawn from h2 to h3.
steps.intro: White to move. Stop ...Bg4, which would pin your knight, with one kingside pawn move.

points: Ask students to say the job of each move out loud
Re1: guard e4
Bb3: keep the bishop alive
c3: make room for d4
h3: stop a pin on the f3 knight
A move with a job beats a random move
mistakes: Moving pieces without a plan
Forgetting that a pin on f3 makes the d4 push harder
Leaving the bishop on a4 after b5
questions: What would a black bishop on g4 do to the f3 knight?
What does the rook on e1 look at?
Why do we want the pawn on d4 later?

steps.intro: A common White plan: push d4 when ready, then bring the b1 knight to d2, f1 and g3.
The c3 pawn supports a later d4. It also gives the bishop room to retreat.

points: White plan: play d4 at the right moment, bring the b1 knight round to g3 through d2 and f1, and keep a safe king
Black plan: attack the white bishop with ...b5, then play ...Na5 or ...Bb7 and push ...c5
The center is not open yet, so slow plans matter more than quick tactics
Do not worry about long theory; know the ideas
mistakes: Rushing d4 before c3
Moving the same piece twice for no reason
Forgetting that the game is long and slow
questions: Why is it fine to move slowly here?
What would the knight on g3 look at?
What does Black want to do with the pawn on c5?

moves.comment: The bishop takes the knight.
Black retakes with the d-pawn. Now Black has two pawns on the c-file.
White castles and keeps a calm, healthy position.

steps.intro: The idea: trade the bishop for the knight. Black's pawns become doubled on the c-file.

moves.comment: Black will have doubled pawns on the c-file.

hints: Use your bishop.
Capture the knight on c6.
steps.intro: White to move. Play the Exchange Variation: take the knight on c6 with your bishop.

hints: Develop the knight, then the bishop to b5.
When Black plays ...a6, take the knight on c6.
Finish by castling.
steps.intro: Play the Exchange Variation as White.

points: White gives the bishop for the knight and doubles Black's c-pawns
Black gets two bishops, but White gets a healthier pawn structure
Later, White often plays d4 to trade pawns and head for a simple, clear game
Names from the openings list: Ruy Lopez: Exchange Variation, Normal Variation
mistakes: Grabbing the e5 pawn at once with the knight
Forgetting to castle
Thinking a trade of bishop for knight loses material. It is an even trade
questions: Why are two pawns on the c-file a weakness?
Who has the two bishops after the trade?
Why is a simple plan good for White here?

steps.intro: After 5.O-O, White has a better pawn shape. Black has doubled pawns on c7 and c6. White plans d4 to open the center.

moves.comment: Safe first.

hints: Use your king.
Castle short, so the king goes to g1.
steps.intro: White to move. Do not rush. Make your king safe before anything else.

points: Black's doubled c-pawns are a long-term weakness
Black has two bishops, so open lines are Black's friend; White tries not to give Black easy play
White's plan: put pieces on good squares, then play d4 to open the center
After d4 and a pawn trade, White has more pawns on the kingside than Black. That can become a winning edge in an endgame
Plan for Black: use the bishops and aim for quick activity
mistakes: Forgetting that the c-pawn weakness only matters in a long game
Opening the center before the pieces are ready
Giving Black easy, quick play
questions: Why does White want the game to last a long time?
Which pawn push opens the center for White?
Why do two bishops like open lines?

moves.comment: White grabs a pawn.
The queen attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4.
The knight goes back.
Black takes the e4 pawn with check. The pawns are level again and the white king is in check.

steps.intro: A tempting move: take the e5 pawn. But watch what the black queen does.
White took e5 but Black took e4. Both sides have seven pawns. So 5.Nxe5 did not win a pawn for free. The calm 5.O-O is better.

points: A pawn grab can look free but may not be
The black queen fork on d4 hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4
White ends up level on pawns, with the king in the middle
A calm 5.O-O avoids all this
mistakes: Taking a pawn before castling
Ignoring the queen's fork
Believing that a capture is always a gain
questions: Which two things does Qd4 attack?
Why is the white king in check at the end?
What is the calm move instead?

chapterList.title: Berlin, Open Spanish and a trap

moves.comment: The Berlin Defence.
Black takes the pawn.
White opens the center.
White wins the pawn back and attacks the knight on d6.
The queens trade with check.
Black's king cannot castle now, but there are no queens to attack it.

steps.intro: The Berlin Defence: Black develops the knight and takes on e4. White opens the center and the queens come off.

moves.comment: A check, and the queens leave the board.

hints: Use your queen.
Capture on d8 with check.
steps.intro: White to move. Trade queens by taking Black's queen with check.

hints: Castle on move four.
Push the d-pawn two squares to open the center.
Take on c6 with the bishop, then take on e5 with the pawn.
steps.intro: Play the Berlin Wall line as White.

points: Black plays 3...Nf6 at once and offers to trade pawns
After 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens are gone
This endgame has a nickname: the Berlin Wall
Black cannot castle but the king is usually safe in an endgame
White can also try the quiet 4.d3, called the Anti-Berlin in the openings list
Keep this chapter short; it is a first look only
mistakes: Panicking when the queens come off
Forgetting that the king can be an active piece in an endgame
Rushing to attack when the position is quiet
questions: Why can the king be safe when queens are gone?
What does it mean that Black cannot castle?
Which side has the two bishops?

moves.comment: Black takes the pawn.
White strikes in the center.
The bishop steps back.
White wins the pawn back and gains space.
A solid support for the d4 square.

steps.intro: In the Open Spanish, Black grabs the e4 pawn right away. White answers by opening the center.

hints: After Black takes e4, push the d-pawn two squares.
When b5 attacks the bishop, go to b3.
Take on e5 with the d-pawn, then play c3.
steps.intro: Play the Open Spanish line as White.

points: Black takes the e4 pawn at once instead of playing ...Be7
White opens the center with d4 and plays for fast piece play
After 8.dxe5 Be6 9.c3 White usually has a space edge and active pieces
Names from the openings list: Ruy Lopez: Open
This is only a first look. Deep theory can wait
mistakes: Trying to win the e4 knight at once
Forgetting to retreat the bishop to b3
Moving the king into danger
questions: Why does White play d4 here?
Where does the bishop go when the b-pawn attacks it?
What does the c3 pawn do in this line?

lessons.title: A trap to avoid: Noah's Ark

moves.comment: This recapture is the real error; it lets ...c5 and ...c4 trap the bishop.
The pawn attacks the queen.
The pawn attacks the bishop. It has no safe way out.

steps.intro: The Noah's Ark Trap. White's bishop on b3 gets locked in by pawns on b5 and c4.
The a4 square is guarded by the b5 pawn. The c4 pawn is guarded by the b5 pawn. The c2 square holds a white pawn. So the bishop is lost for a pawn or two. Playing c3 first would have given it room.

points: This trap is against White: it is a lesson in what not to do
White pushes d4 early (a riskier move order), trades pieces, and the white bishop on b3 is shut in by Black's pawns
The openings list names it Ruy Lopez: Noah's Ark Trap
Safer for White: play c3 first, so the bishop has c2 to go to
mistakes: Pushing d4 before c3 is a riskier move order when the bishop is on b3
Forgetting to check where the bishop can escape
Taking back on d4 with the queen when ...c5 and ...c4 can trap your bishop
questions: Which black pawns box in the bishop?
Which square would be free if White had played c3 first?
Before we push a pawn, what should we ask about our bishop?
